cards.front: {{c1::Tonicity}} is the part of osmolality made by solutes that do not cross cell membranes freely.
cards.back: Only these solutes pull water into or out of cells.
cards.quote: Tonicity is the part of osmolality made by solutes that do not cross cell membranes freely.
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: Why does adding urea to plasma raise osmolality but add almost nothing to tonicity?
cards.back: Urea crosses cell membranes, so it does not pull water out of cells. Only solutes that do not cross freely create tonicity.
cards.quote: urea, which crosses cell membranes, raises osmolality but adds almost nothing to tonicity
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: Why is plasma sodium concentration close to (exchangeable sodium + exchangeable potassium) divided by total body water?
cards.back: Water equalizes osmolality across compartments. Sodium holds extracellular water and potassium holds cell water, and cell water is part of the denominator.
cards.quote: Cells hold their water mainly with potassium, and the extracellular fluid holds its water mainly with sodium.
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: A 70 kg adult has 42 L of body water (14 L extracellular) and plasma sodium of 140 mmol per L. They drink 1 L of plain water. Estimate the new plasma sodium concentration and how much of the litre stays outside cells.
cards.back: Solute unchanged, water now 43 L: 140 × 42/43 ≈ 137 mmol per L. Water spreads through all body water, so only 14/42, about a third of a litre, stays extracellular.
cards.quote: The solute has not changed, so the concentration falls from 140 to about 137 mmol per L.
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: In a 70 kg adult with plasma sodium 140 mmol per L, 1 L of fluid at plasma sodium strength is given instead of plain water. What happens to plasma sodium concentration and to extracellular volume?
cards.back: Concentration does not move, and extracellular fluid gains the whole litre.
cards.why: Fluid at plasma strength has no osmotic pull on cells, so none of it enters them.
cards.quote: The fluid at plasma strength has no osmotic pull on the cells, so the whole litre stays outside them and the concentration does not move.
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: A person loses 1 L of sweat with sodium taken as 50 mmol per L. Sweat carries sodium out of the body. Which way does plasma sodium concentration move, and why?
cards.back: It rises (to about 142 mmol per L in a 70 kg adult starting at 140).
cards.why: Sweat is far weaker than plasma, so it removes water out of proportion to solute.
cards.quote: so it removes water out of proportion to solute and plasma sodium concentration rises
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: In the water loop, what senses plasma tonicity, and what two effectors does it drive?
cards.back: Osmoreceptor neurons in the lamina terminalis (OVLT); they drive thirst and vasopressin release.
cards.quote: Osmoreceptor neurons in the lamina terminalis sense plasma tonicity and drive thirst and the release of vasopressin
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: The sodium loop's sensors (arterial and atrial baroreceptors, afferent arteriole stretch, macula densa salt delivery) read {{c1::effective circulating volume}}: how well the arteries are filled.
cards.quote: Its sensors read effective circulating volume: how well the arteries are filled
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: With the water loop holding plasma sodium at 140 mmol per L, a healthy adult keeps an extra 280 mmol of sodium. About how much does extracellular fluid (and body weight) change?
cards.back: 280 / 140 mmol per L = 2 L of extracellular fluid, about 2 kg of weight gained.
cards.why: The water loop holds back water until the ratio is restored, so each 140 mmol kept carries about 1 L.
cards.quote: every 140 mmol or so of sodium the body keeps carries about 1 L of extracellular fluid, so the sodium loop sets volume by setting sodium content.
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: A healthy-kidney adult has a low plasma sodium concentration. What does that say about total body sodium?
cards.back: Nothing on its own: it means too much water for the solute. Total body sodium can be low, normal or high.
cards.quote: So a low sodium concentration means too much water for the solute, with total body sodium low, normal or high
cards.section: Water sets the concentration; sodium sets the volume

cards.front: How does vasopressin acting on collecting-duct principal cells make the duct permeable to water?
cards.back: It binds basolateral V2 receptors and raises cyclic AMP; aquaporin-2 moves from vesicles into the apical membrane, and water leaves down the medullary gradient.
cards.quote: vasopressin binds the V2 receptor on the basolateral membrane of principal cells and raises cyclic AMP
cards.section: Vasopressin opens the collecting duct, and thirst replaces the water

cards.front: A water-deprived adult human makes urine at about {{c1::1,000 to 1,200}} mOsm per kg; with vasopressin absent, urine can fall near 50.
cards.quote: A water-deprived adult human makes urine at about 1,000 to 1,200 mOsm per kg
cards.section: Vasopressin opens the collecting duct, and thirst replaces the water

cards.front: Aquaporin-2 is deleted in adult mice. Urine output rises from about 2 to 25 mL per day, urine osmolality falls from about 2,000 to below 500 mosmol per kg and does not rise after water deprivation. What does this show?
cards.back: Aquaporin-2 is required: without it, vasopressin cannot make the collecting duct permeable to water.
cards.quote: in mice with aquaporin-2 deleted, vasopressin cannot make the collecting duct permeable to water at all
cards.section: Vasopressin opens the collecting duct, and thirst replaces the water

cards.front: How do vasopressin and thirst divide the work of defending plasma osmolality?
cards.back: Vasopressin is the fast renal defence that cuts renal water loss to a minimum; thirst replaces the water already lost.
cards.quote: vasopressin is the fast renal defence, which cuts renal water loss to a minimum, and thirst replaces the water already lost
cards.section: Vasopressin opens the collecting duct, and thirst replaces the water

cards.front: In ten healthy volunteers given hypertonic saline, the regression threshold for vasopressin release was 285 mosmol per kg with a slope of 0.4 pmol per L per mosmol per kg. Predict the rise in plasma vasopressin when plasma osmolality reaches 290.
cards.back: (290 − 285) × 0.4 = 2.0 pmol per L above threshold.
cards.quote: the regression threshold for vasopressin release was 285, with slopes of 0.3 cm of scale and 0.4 pmol per L per mosmol per kg above those thresholds
cards.section: Osmoreceptors and thresholds

cards.front: Osmolar clearance, the urine flow that would carry the excreted solute at plasma concentration, is Cosm = {{c1::Uosm × V / Posm}}.
cards.back: Divide by plasma, not urine, osmolality.
cards.quote: That flow is the osmolar clearance, Cosm: the urine flow that would carry the excreted solute if urine were as concentrated as plasma.
cards.section: Free-water clearance splits urine into two parts

cards.front: Free-water clearance, the part of urine flow that carried no solute, is CH2O = {{c1::V − Cosm}}.
cards.back: V is urine flow.
cards.quote: Whatever flow is left over, V − Cosm, carried no solute at all.
cards.section: Free-water clearance splits urine into two parts

cards.front: What does a positive, zero or negative free-water clearance mean about the urine?
cards.back: Positive: urine more dilute than plasma. Zero: isosmotic urine. Negative: concentrated urine, with minus CH2O the solute-free water returned to blood (TcH2O).
cards.quote: A positive CH2O means urine more dilute than plasma, zero means isosmotic urine, and a negative value means concentrated urine.
cards.section: Free-water clearance splits urine into two parts

cards.front: A healthy adult's timed collection: urine flow 2.0 mL per min, urine osmolality 840 mOsm per kg, plasma osmolality 280 mOsm per kg. Find Cosm, CH2O and TcH2O.
cards.back: Cosm = 840 × 2.0 / 280 = 6.0 mL per min. CH2O = 2.0 − 6.0 = −4.0 mL per min. TcH2O = +4.0 mL per min returned to blood.
cards.quote: When it is negative, minus CH2O is the solute-free water reabsorbed into blood (TcH2O).
cards.section: Free-water clearance splits urine into two parts

cards.front: A volunteer has plasma osmolality 265 mOsm per kg yet makes urine at 500 mOsm per kg. What does the mismatch tell you?
cards.back: Something other than osmolality is holding vasopressin on.
cards.why: Dilute plasma should switch osmotic vasopressin release off. Causes include injected hormone, or in patients volume loss, nausea, pain or a tumour.
cards.quote: Something other than osmolality is holding vasopressin on
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the urine

cards.front: Solute excretion is 720 mOsm per day. What are the smallest daily urine volume at a maximal urine osmolality of 1,200 mOsm per kg, and the largest at a very dilute 60 mOsm per kg?
cards.back: 720 / 1,200 = 0.6 L per day; 720 / 60 = 12 L per day. Solute delivery limits water excretion as well as vasopressin.
cards.quote: Water excretion is limited by solute delivery as well as by vasopressin.
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the urine

cards.front: Why can free-water clearance mislead about where plasma sodium concentration is heading?
cards.back: It is a solute-based index of one collection that counts urea and other ineffective osmoles, so it cannot say which way plasma sodium concentration will move next.
cards.quote: it cannot say which way plasma sodium concentration will move next
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the urine

cards.front: Urine flow 2.0 mL per min, urine osmolality 600 mOsm per kg (mostly urea), urine sodium plus potassium 70 mmol per L, plasma osmolality 300 mOsm per kg, plasma sodium 140 mmol per L. Compute CH2O and electrolyte-free water clearance, and say which way the urine pushes plasma sodium concentration.
cards.back: Cosm = 600 × 2.0 / 300 = 4.0, so CH2O = −2.0 mL per min. Electrolyte-free water clearance = 2.0 × (1 − 70/140) = +1.0 mL per min, so the urine pushes plasma sodium concentration up.
cards.why: Urea is an ineffective osmole; the electrolyte split tracks the effect on sodium concentration.
cards.quote: the same split made with urine sodium plus potassium against plasma sodium, describes the effect on sodium concentration better
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the urine

cards.front: What are the three inputs to renin release from granular cells of the afferent arteriole?
cards.back: A fall in renal perfusion pressure, a fall in sodium chloride at the macula densa, and sympathetic stimulation of beta-adrenergic receptors on the granular cells.
cards.quote: The sodium loop starts with renin release from granular cells of the afferent arteriole, which has three inputs
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: What two actions of angiotensin II raise sodium retention?
cards.back: It raises proximal sodium reabsorption and stimulates aldosterone release.
cards.quote: Renin leads to angiotensin II, which raises proximal sodium reabsorption and stimulates aldosterone release.
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: Besides angiotensin II, aldosterone release is raised directly by a rise in plasma {{c1::potassium}}.
cards.quote: it is also raised directly by a rise in plasma potassium
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: What mainly triggers atrial natriuretic peptide release, and how does it lower blood pressure?
cards.back: Rising atrial-wall stretch with intravascular volume. It causes natriuresis and diuresis, vasorelaxation, and antagonism of the renin-angiotensin system.
cards.quote: atrial natriuretic peptide is released from atrial granules mainly when atrial-wall stretch rises with intravascular volume
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: After a modest blood loss in a healthy person, renin rises. Why does plasma sodium concentration not move at first?
cards.back: Blood is lost at plasma strength, so the solute-to-water ratio is unchanged; only volume fell.
cards.quote: Plasma sodium concentration at first does not move: blood is lost at plasma strength, so the ratio is unchanged.
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: Two normal men on constant diets received large daily doses of aldosterone. Weight rose for some days, then levelled off while the hormone continued, with urinary sodium back near control and only slight oedema. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: Aldosterone is not the sole setter of sodium excretion: once extracellular volume expands, other mechanisms restore excretion (escape). It does not show which mechanisms; that is still argued.
cards.why: A levelling weight fits a fixed amount of sodium kept (about 1 kg per 140 mmol), then intake matched by excretion.
cards.quote: Sodium was retained and weight rose at first; then urinary sodium climbed back to about the control level, oedema stayed slight, and the weight gain stopped.
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: A person loses a large volume of blood, then drinks plain water. Predict vasopressin and plasma sodium concentration, and name the rule that breaks.
cards.back: Vasopressin stays high even as plasma becomes dilute, the kidney keeps water, and plasma sodium concentration falls.
cards.why: With large volume loss, vasopressin follows volume, not osmolality, so the two loops collide.
cards.quote: so when volume loss is large it follows volume, not osmolality
cards.section: The sodium loop sets volume, and aldosterone escapes

cards.front: About {{c1::98 percent}} of body potassium is inside cells, mostly in skeletal muscle.
cards.back: Extracellular potassium is 3.5 to 5 mEq per L.
cards.quote: about 98 percent, mostly in skeletal muscle
cards.section: Potassium is shifted in minutes and excreted over hours

cards.front: A 70 kg adult has 14 L of extracellular fluid at a potassium concentration of 4.2 mEq per L. They absorb 21 mEq of potassium and, hypothetically, none enters cells and none is excreted. Estimate plasma potassium.
cards.back: 21 mEq / 14 L = 1.5 mEq per L rise, from 4.2 to about 5.7 mEq per L.
cards.why: The extracellular pool is small (about 59 mEq), so a meal's potassium would shift its concentration a lot without uptake into cells.
cards.quote: 30 mEq spread through 14 L is about 2.1 mEq per L
cards.section: Potassium is shifted in minutes and excreted over hours

cards.front: What are the two time courses by which the body defends plasma potassium?
cards.back: First by shifting potassium into cells, in minutes; then by renal secretion, over hours.
cards.quote: it is defended first by shifting into cells, in minutes, then by renal secretion, over hours.
cards.section: Potassium is shifted in minutes and excreted over hours

cards.front: Which two hormones drive potassium into muscle, through which pump, and via which receptor for the catecholamine?
cards.back: Insulin (directly) and epinephrine (through beta2-adrenergic receptors), both by stimulating the Na+-K+-ATPase.
cards.quote: insulin directly, and epinephrine through beta2-adrenergic receptors
cards.section: The shift: minutes

cards.front: Insulin is given to a potassium-deprived rat and to a control rat. Which shows the smaller fall in plasma potassium, and why?
cards.back: The potassium-deprived rat.
cards.why: Its muscle becomes resistant to insulin's stimulation of potassium uptake, so less potassium moves into cells.
cards.quote: their muscle becomes resistant to insulin's stimulation of potassium uptake
cards.section: The shift: minutes

cards.front: Equal acid loads are given as a mineral acid or as an organic acid. Which shifts more potassium out of cells?
cards.back: The mineral acid, by far.
cards.why: The shift depends on the acid, and it is not a direct potassium-for-hydrogen exchange.
cards.quote: mineral-acid loading moves far more out of cells than organic-acid loading, and the shift is not a direct potassium-for-hydrogen exchange
cards.section: The shift: minutes

cards.front: Why is the part of urinary potassium that rises with intake attributed to secretion rather than filtration?
cards.back: Less than 10 percent of filtered potassium reaches the distal nephron, a fraction that changes little with diet, yet on high intake urinary potassium exceeds that amount.
cards.quote: So the part of urinary potassium that rises with intake is secreted, by principal cells
cards.section: Secretion: hours

cards.front: How do principal cells secrete potassium into the collecting-duct lumen?
cards.back: They take it in across the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase and release it to the lumen through ROMK; at high flow, flow-activated BK channels add more.
cards.quote: take it in across the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase and release it to the lumen through ROMK
cards.section: Secretion: hours

cards.front: Delivery of sodium and water to the distal secretory cells rises while aldosterone is unchanged. Predict potassium secretion.
cards.back: It rises.
cards.why: Delivery of sodium and water is one of the two major influences on secretion, with higher flow raising it.
cards.quote: delivery of sodium and water to the secretory cells, with higher flow raising secretion
cards.section: Secretion: hours

cards.front: Aldosterone is high both in low volume and in high plasma potassium. Why is potassium secretion not raised in low volume?
cards.back: Low volume brings low sodium and water delivery and high angiotensin II, which restrains potassium secretion. In high potassium, delivery is normal or higher and potassium itself stimulates secretion.
cards.quote: Low volume brings low delivery and high angiotensin II, which also restrains potassium secretion, so secretion is not raised.
cards.section: One hormone, two outcomes: the aldosterone paradox

cards.front: Mice eat a low-potassium diet, even with high salt. What happens to NCC in the distal convoluted tubule, and how is potassium secretion then reduced?
cards.back: NCC is activated even on high salt. The proposed chain: low plasma potassium hyperpolarizes the distal cell, chloride falls, WNK kinases switch on NCC, so less sodium and water reach secretory cells and potassium secretion falls.
cards.why: The mouse result was NCC activation with sodium retention and raised blood pressure; the voltage and chloride steps come from cell experiments, and reduced delivery is the authors' account.
cards.quote: More sodium is then taken back upstream, less sodium and water reach the secretory cells, and potassium secretion falls.
cards.section: One hormone, two outcomes: the aldosterone paradox

cards.front: Epinephrine lowered plasma potassium in healthy volunteers, and a beta2-selective antagonist prevented the fall. Predict the result with a beta1-selective antagonist, and say what the blockade data cannot show.
cards.back: The fall should largely persist under beta1 block (a prediction, not a result). Blockade shows beta2 is required here, not that it sets plasma potassium minute by minute in daily life, nor which tissue took the potassium up.
cards.quote: Under beta1 block it should largely persist, because the receptor carrying the effect here was beta2
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: During an epinephrine infusion, plasma potassium falls. What paired measurement over the same minutes would show the potassium moved into cells rather than leaving the body?
cards.back: Urinary potassium unchanged while plasma potassium falls, with intake, extracellular volume and non-renal losses controlled.
cards.quote: urinary potassium unchanged while plasma potassium falls supports a shift into cells rather than a loss from the body
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A patient with a potassium deficit and low plasma sodium receives potassium only, no sodium. Predict plasma sodium concentration.
cards.back: It rises.
cards.why: In simplified form, plasma sodium concentration is (exchangeable sodium + exchangeable potassium) / total body water, so potassium sits in the numerator.
cards.quote: Because potassium sits in the numerator, replacing a potassium deficit raises plasma sodium concentration too.
cards.section: How the ratio was measured

cards.front: In heart failure, extracellular fluid is expanded. Predict whether the sodium loop signals for sodium excretion or retention, and why.
cards.back: Retention.
cards.why: The loop reads effective circulating volume (arterial filling), which reads underfilled, not extracellular volume.
cards.quote: so the sodium loop keeps signalling for sodium retention
cards.section: When effective volume and extracellular volume part company

cards.front: Plasma glucose rises very high (or mannitol is infused). Predict plasma osmolality and plasma sodium concentration.
cards.back: Osmolality rises while sodium concentration falls.
cards.why: The added effective solute draws water out of cells, diluting plasma sodium.
cards.quote: glucose (when it is high) or mannitol adds tonicity, draws water out of cells, and lowers plasma sodium concentration while plasma osmolality rises
cards.section: When effective volume and extracellular volume part company
